personas.why: Seeing the system refuse to judge a knee it can't see is more interesting than another AI success demo. The support-jobs line catches me just as I'm about to swipe, though I'd be more likely to discuss it than try FORM.
One red tile out of 23 gives me a clear question: why that one? When the clip switches to a pulldown and then a lunge, I lose track of the set I wanted explained.
I can see the swing without understanding either angle, and I have a friend who does it. But 'The wait is over' sounds like an announcement for followers. I wasn't waiting for anything.
The red gap gets me past three seconds. Once he says he was swinging his legs, I think I've got the answer; a countdown isn't a reason to stay.
I like 'every dip is a rep' because I can check it with my eyes. Just as I understand the wave, it disappears into labelled boxes, and watching starts to feel like studying.

The skeleton turning into a signal makes this feel like a project I could actually build. I'd comment FORM for the diagram and send it to a project teammate. The Bangalore role keeps me through the last frame.
I stay because the camera turn shows how a convincing number can be misleading. Once both checks land on the original red tile, I've got the answer; the second STOP stamp feels like the end.
Showing the false alarm earns my attention. But two judges using the same camera view can agree and still be wrong. I'd rather see how often they disagreed than another diagram explaining the rule.
The turned lunge makes the judge-versus-coach diagram worth saving: I can explain why the second check exists. When Salesforce comes up over the gym footage, I assume the reel I wanted is over.
CHECK FOOTAGE is the interesting outcome: the system can hand back a doubtful call. Returning to the crunch confirms what frame one already showed me, so I leave at the stamp.
I'd send the ghost-versus-real rep to my gym group because nobody needs the audio to get it. But 'access my form-coach skill' doesn't tell me whether I can use it on my phone, so I don't comment.
The green ghost over the red rep is the image I'd remember tomorrow. By the elbow wave I'm reading labels instead of watching someone struggle through a rep; the human bit was more fun.
Rep table plus key frames versus frames alone is specific enough to make me want the implementation. I'd comment FORM for it. The hiring teaser arrives after I've already taken the action I came for.

The turned lunge is the clip I'd send a colleague: the apparent depth changes even though the movement is consistent. I'd stay for the post-training role, but the two-model agreement alone wouldn't make me trust the form verdict.

I'd show a client the raw swing next to the ghost; that's easier than talking through hip angles. 'Always film from the side' loses me. This clip shows why turning mid-lunge mattered, not the right view for every exercise.
The chant and the wall snapping onto one red set keep me watching. I want to see that tile open and the bad rep play. Instead I get '17 joints, 30 frames a second.'
